newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain suffers as Eurospotlight shifts to politics.
newsitem.headline: Spain suffers as Eurospotlight shifts to politics.

text.p: Spanish financial markets tumbled on Monday as jubilence over economic accomplishments gave way to dismay that political factors might still prevent it from joining the launch of Europe's single currency.

Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar had focused the nation's EMU drive on its economic accomplishments, in an attempt to disengage Spain's political status from the more politically powerful but economically weak-kneed Italy.

But the European Union's power brokers clearly are finding it difficult to exclude Italy, a founding member of the European Union and a Group of Seven member, while admitting the lesser power, Spain -- regardless of its paper credentials.
On Monday, the peseta tumbled past 85.00 per mark for the first time since August, while the 10-year bond future fell 90 basis points to a low of 113.10 and stocks eased.

In recent months, Spanish markets had gained ground dramatically, as a consensus built that the nation and its new conservative government had done their economic homework and kicked the nation into economic shape for the single currency.
Inflation tumbled, long-term interest rates fell, the peseta steadied and the government tightened up the budget, narrowed the deficit, and set to work on Spain's debt.
But last week, Juergen Stark, the number two at Germany's Finance Ministry, said merely fulfilling the economic goals simply wasn't good enough to get in at the start.
And Spain's hopes began to crumble.

Early Monday, a top German banker said the debate about Italy and Spain's EMU chances was unsettling markets and it would be better to announce soon that only a small block of countries would go forward and thus calm markets.
His comments followed remarks over the weekend by other German bankers who held out the prospect of turmoil on financial markets if countries like Italy joined from the start.
"It's difficult to square this one. If there is no special deal of Italy, Spain and Portugal later, then Italy will not want to be left out," said Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC.
For Spain, its options are now limited, economists say.
"Aznar is playing his cards correctly," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America in Madrid. "But he can't do much for his own gain."
If Aznar continues to push, he could endanger the entire project. "It would be a phyrric victory," Lumholdt said.

Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid, said Spain could try to counterattack, launching talks with Italy and Portugal to join in a common cause -- a suggestion Italy made last autumn.
